I'm part of the Reddit exodus. I'm excited to be here, and a little saddened and frustrated.

Every site has it's own appeal and downsides - I get that. Reddit has become a different place (granted I wasn't there from the beginning, but I still see the changes). Part of me likes the upvote/downvote system - part of me likes 4chan since you can say what you please and it can't be downvoted out of sight, but even that place is being really heavily modded.

I feel like that is the doom of every site that gets big enough to draw attention. Get noticed, get acquired, get used for adverts/bring on the shills, get policed, become what you said you would never be.

I worry about the online communities I'm a part of as I see them become more and more 'politically correct.' is this the world we live in? Everyone so up in arms about their fee-fees getting hurt that they can't participate in open conversation? Speak your mind, but if you offend me - I will doxx/downvote you to kingdom come. Really? That's what we are now? Silence everyone who doesn't agree! I know this is not true across the board, I'm sure there are plenty of arenas where you can have great, informative, respectful conversations - but this is the trend I see.

But hey, I signed up here. I must have some hope, right? I don't have grand aspirations of being a part of the next big wave - I just skulk around not really contributing anything.

Apologies if this sounds trite. I really don't know why I typed this all out. Thinking a lot about the state of things - life, govt (US here), future shit.

Welcome aboard, Spindle_spire! We have similar concerns about free speech. Glad to see you here.

Here is a related conversation I had earlier today with anonycon, another Reddit expat:

"The second reason I don't care is that I don't consider Reddit important enough to make unfettered free speech an absolute necessity" -anonycon

This get's close to my real concerns. Where is it that free speech and the airing of opinions and the arguments by the electorate are to take place in an open and honest manner? The bar? The real public square where no one actually goes?

No. Online is the real public square whether we like it or not.

Is that something you have come to realize, anonycon?

Is VOAT a substitute for Reddit yet? In order to be fully equivalent to "the public forum/square" you need to have enough participation from your own country and locality. The more you have a potential audience of voters, the more meaningful the conversation becomes in a practical sense. Of course, we all individually take home lessons and ideas from any conversation but the greater impact on democracy is what should interest all of us. The sharing of ideas and opinions and having them challenged or affirmed impacts democracy in a good way, it seems to me. Online can impact real life.

Yet here is the online pattern. Consider this.In the space of a few years we have seen Huffpo, Dig, 4Chan, and now Reddit, etc blossoming into real town squares of sorts with a large participant base only to see...BAM! The rug of free speech is yanked out.

As the critical mass is reached then the owners/managers take away the free-speech charter and leverage their website's size and popularity for some undisclosed and undemocratic financial interests. As a user, you only know that the shift has occurred when the MODS and Censorship and Banning and thought control regimes are rolled out as quietly as possible and each person is left to figure out the new, undemocratic and often fascist/agenda-driven rules-changes.

This is a problem and I hope you can see it. The town square and its communities are under a continuous process of being raided and dispersed.

I asked "where is the public square?". I argue that these deliberate breaks in the continuity of discussion-communities are destructive, not just in an online context, but IRL.

How is your real life democracy functioning?

How do you know that the horribly dysfunctional and feckless real life responses we see from the citizenry is not partly due to the disruption of online communities?

I'm not saying that there are not a hundred other factors for why public policy no longer reflects the public will. I am just saying that the continuous disruptions do have repercussions IRL. I've lost track of hundreds of users over the years. And each time the boom on free speech is lowered as at reddit, I have been left to search blindly for the next town square. And I almost never reconnect with those I lost in the transition.
